title: 14. Glory to the rooster!
paragraphs: His nerves gave out, as they say, and Rimsky did not wait for the report to be finished but fled to his office. He sat at his desk, staring with inflamed eyes at the magic ten-rouble notes lying in front of him. The financial director’s mind was reeling. Outside, a steady roar rolled on. The audience was pouring out of the Variety building into the street in streams. Suddenly the financial director’s extraordinarily sharpened hearing caught the distinct trill of a police whistle. In itself that sound never promises anything pleasant. And when it was repeated, and a second whistle, more commanding and more prolonged, came to its aid, and then a clearly audible guffawing joined in, and even some sort of hooting and whooping, the financial director understood at once that something else scandalous and nasty had happened in the street. And that this, however much one might like to wave it away, was most intimately connected with the disgusting performance given by the black magician and his assistants. The sensitive financial director was not in the least mistaken.
The moment he glanced out of the window that looked onto Sadovaya, his face twisted, and he did not whisper but hissed:
“I knew it!”

In the bright light of the powerful street lamps he saw on the pavement below him a lady wearing nothing but a slip and a pair of violet knickers. True, the lady had a little hat on her head and an umbrella in her hands.

Around this lady, who was in a state of utter confusion, now crouching down, now making as if to run off somewhere, a crowd surged, giving off that very laughter which sent a chill down the financial director’s spine. Next to the lady some citizen was rushing about, tearing off his summer coat and, in his agitation, quite unable to manage the sleeve, in which his arm had got stuck.

Shouts and roaring laughter came from another spot as well—namely from the left entrance—and, turning his head that way, Grigory Danilovich saw a second lady, in pink underwear. She leaped from the roadway onto the pavement, trying to hide in the doorway, but the audience streaming out blocked her way, and the poor victim of her own frivolity and passion for clothes, deceived by the firm of the vile Fagot, dreamed of only one thing—of sinking through the earth. A policeman was rushing toward the unfortunate woman, drilling the air with his whistle, and behind the policeman hurried some exceedingly merry young men in caps. It was they who were giving off that very laughter and hooting.
A thin, mustached cabby flew up to the first undressed lady and reined in his bony, broken-down horse with a flourish. The mustached man’s face was grinning with joy.
Rimsky struck himself on the head with his fist, spat, and sprang back from the window.

He sat at the desk for some time, listening to the street. The whistling at various points reached its height and then began to die down. The scandal, to Rimsky’s surprise, was somehow cleared up unexpectedly quickly.

The time had come to act; he would have to drink the bitter cup of responsibility. The telephones had been repaired during the third part of the show; he would have to call, report what had happened, ask for help, lie his way out, blame everything on Likhodeyev, shield himself, and so on. Pah, the devil!

Twice the upset director put his hand on the receiver, and twice he took it away again. And suddenly, in the dead silence of the office, the telephone itself burst out ringing right in the financial director’s face, and he started and went cold. “My nerves are in a fine state, though,” he thought, and picked up the receiver. At once he recoiled from it and turned whiter than paper. A quiet, at the same time insinuating and depraved woman’s voice whispered into the receiver:
“Don’t call anyone, Rimsky, or it will go badly...”

The line instantly went empty. Feeling goose bumps crawl down his back, the financial director put down the receiver and for some reason looked round at the window behind him. Through the sparse branches of the maple, still only faintly covered in green, he saw the moon racing through a transparent little cloud. For some reason his eyes fastened on the branches, and Rimsky looked at them, and the longer he looked, the more and more strongly fear took hold of him.

With an effort, the financial director at last turned away from the moonlit window and stood up. There could no longer be any question of telephoning, and now the financial director thought of only one thing—how to get out of the theater as quickly as possible.

He listened: the theater building was silent. Rimsky realized that he had long been alone on the whole second floor, and at this thought a childish, irresistible fear seized him. He could not think without a shudder that he would now have to walk alone along the empty corridors and go down the stairs. Feverishly he snatched the hypnotist’s ten-rouble notes from the desk, hid them in his briefcase, and coughed to cheer himself up even a tiny bit. The cough came out hoarse and weak.

And here it seemed to him that a rotten dampness was suddenly seeping in from under the office door. A shiver ran down the financial director’s spine. And then, on top of that, the clock unexpectedly struck and began to chime midnight. And even the chiming made the financial director shiver. But his heart sank completely when he heard a latchkey quietly turning in the lock of the door. Clutching his briefcase with damp, cold hands, the financial director felt that if this rustling in the keyhole lasted a little longer, he would not be able to bear it and would give a piercing scream.

At last the door yielded to someone’s efforts, opened, and Varenukha came noiselessly into the office. Rimsky sat down in the armchair just where he stood, because his legs gave way. Drawing a breath into his chest, he smiled a sort of ingratiating smile and said softly:
“God, how you frightened me...”
Yes, this sudden appearance could have frightened anyone, and yet at the same time it was a great joy: at least one loose end had stuck out in this tangled business.
“Well, speak, quickly! Well! Well!” Rimsky croaked, clutching at this loose end. “What does all this mean?!”
“Forgive me, please,” the newcomer responded in a hollow voice, closing the door, “I thought you’d already gone.”
And Varenukha, without taking off his cap, walked over to the armchair and sat down on the other side of the desk.

It must be said that Varenukha’s answer showed a slight oddity, which at once pricked the financial director, whose sensitivity could rival the seismograph of any of the best stations in the world. How could that be? Why would Varenukha come to the financial director’s office if he supposed he was not there? After all, he had his own office. That was one. And second: whichever entrance Varenukha had come into the building by, he would inevitably have met one of the night watchmen, and they had all been told that Grigory Danilovich would be staying on in his office for a while.
But the financial director did not ponder this oddity for long. He had no time for that.
“Why didn’t you call? What’s all this nonsense with Yalta about?”
“Well, just what I said,” replied the administrator, smacking his lips as though a bad tooth were bothering him. “They found him in a tavern in Pushkino.”
“What do you mean, in Pushkino?! That’s just outside Moscow? And the telegrams from Yalta?!”
“Yalta, the devil it was! He got the Pushkino telegraph clerk drunk, and the two of them started making mischief, including sending telegrams marked ‘Yalta.’”

“Aha... aha... Well, all right, all right...” Rimsky did not so much say as sing. His eyes lit up with a little yellow light. In his head a festive picture took shape: Styopa’s shameful dismissal from his post. Liberation! The financial director’s long-awaited liberation from this calamity in the person of Likhodeyev! And perhaps Stepan Bogdanovich would earn himself something even worse than dismissal... “Details!” said Rimsky, banging the paperweight on the desk.

And Varenukha began to give the details. As soon as he had arrived where the financial director had sent him, he was received at once and listened to with the utmost attention. Of course, nobody so much as entertained the thought that Styopa might be in Yalta. Everyone immediately agreed with Varenukha’s suggestion that Likhodeyev was, of course, at the “Yalta” in Pushkino.
“So where is he now?” the agitated financial director interrupted the administrator.
“Well, where else would he be?” answered the administrator with a crooked grin. “In the sobering-up station, naturally.”
“Well, well! Oh, thank you!”

And Varenukha went on with his tale. And the more he told, the more vividly there unrolled before the financial director a very long chain of Likhodeyev’s boorish acts and outrages, and every link in this chain was worse than the one before. What a thing it was, for a start, the drunken dance arm in arm with the telegraph clerk on the lawn in front of the Pushkino telegraph office, to the strains of some vagrant accordion! The chase after some citizenesses squealing with terror! The attempt to pick a fight with the barman in the “Yalta” itself! The scattering of green onions over the floor of that same “Yalta.” The smashing of eight bottles of dry white Ai-Danil. The breaking of the meter of a taxi driver who had refused to give Styopa his car. The threat to arrest the citizens who tried to put a stop to Styopa’s filthy antics... In a word, sheer black horror!

Styopa was well known in the theatrical circles of Moscow, and everyone knew that the man was no gift. But all the same, what the administrator was telling about him was too much even for Styopa. Yes, too much. Even very much too much...

Rimsky’s prickly eyes cut across the desk into the administrator’s face, and the further he went, the darker those eyes became. The more lifelike and colorful the vile details with which the administrator decked out his story, the less the financial director believed the storyteller. And when Varenukha reported that Styopa had run so wild that he had tried to resist those who had come to take him back to Moscow, the financial director already knew for certain that everything the administrator, returning at midnight, was telling him—everything—was a lie! A lie from the first word to the last.

Varenukha had not gone to Pushkino, and Styopa himself had not been in Pushkino either. There had been no drunken telegraph clerk, no broken glass in the tavern, Styopa had not been tied up with ropes...—none of it had happened.

The moment the financial director became firmly convinced that the administrator was lying to him, fear crept over his body, starting at his feet, and twice, once again, the financial director fancied that a rotten, malarial dampness was drifting along the floor. Never for an instant taking his eyes off the administrator, who was writhing somehow strangely in the armchair, all the time trying not to move out of the blue shadow of the desk lamp, and shielding himself in a remarkable way with a newspaper, supposedly from the light of the bulb, which was bothering him—the financial director thought of only one thing: what on earth did all this mean? Why was the administrator, who had come back to him far too late, lying to him so brazenly in the deserted and silent building? And an awareness of danger, an unknown but menacing danger, began to oppress the financial director’s soul. Pretending not to notice the administrator’s dodges and his tricks with the newspaper, the financial director studied his face, hardly listening any longer to what Varenukha was spinning. There was something that seemed even more inexplicable than the slanderous tale of adventures in Pushkino, invented for who knew what purpose, and that something was a change in the administrator’s appearance and manners.

However much he pulled the duck-bill peak of his cap down over his eyes to cast a shadow on his face, however much he twisted the newspaper sheet about, the financial director managed to make out an enormous bruise on the right side of his face, right by the nose. Besides that, the administrator, usually full-blooded, was now pale with a chalky, unhealthy pallor, and on this stifling night an old striped scarf had for some reason been wound around his neck. And if to this one added the disgusting habit of sucking and smacking his lips, which the administrator had acquired during his absence, the sharp change in his voice, which had become hollow and coarse, and the furtive cowardice in his eyes, one could safely say that Ivan Savelyevich Varenukha had become unrecognizable.

Something else was burningly troubling the financial director, but what exactly he could not make out, however much he strained his inflamed brain, however hard he peered at Varenukha. One thing he could affirm: there was something unheard-of, something unnatural, in this combination of the administrator and the all too familiar armchair.
“Well, we got the better of him at last, loaded him into the car,” droned Varenukha, peeping out from behind the sheet and covering the bruise with his palm.

Rimsky suddenly stretched out his hand and, as if absent-mindedly, drumming his fingers on the desk at the same time, pressed the button of the electric bell with his palm—and froze. In the empty building the sharp signal would certainly have been heard. But no signal followed, and the button sank lifelessly into the desktop. The button was dead, the bell broken.
The financial director’s ruse did not escape Varenukha, who asked, with a twitch, and an unmistakable spiteful fire flickering in his eyes:
“What are you ringing for?”
“Absent-mindedly,” the financial director replied hollowly, jerking his hand back, and in his turn asked in an unsteady voice: “What’s that on your face?”
“The car skidded, I hit myself on the door handle,” answered Varenukha, looking away.
“He’s lying!” the financial director exclaimed in his mind. And then suddenly his eyes grew round and utterly mad, and he stared at the back of the armchair.

Behind the armchair, on the floor, lay two crossed shadows, one denser and blacker, the other faint and gray. The shadow of the chair’s back and its tapered legs could be seen distinctly on the floor, but above the back there was no shadow of Varenukha’s head on the floor, just as under the legs there were no feet of the administrator.
“He casts no shadow!” Rimsky cried out desperately in his mind. A fit of trembling struck him.
Varenukha glanced furtively behind the back of the armchair, following Rimsky’s mad gaze, and understood that he had been found out.
He rose from the armchair (the financial director did the same) and stepped back a pace from the desk, clutching the briefcase in his hands.

“You’ve guessed, damn you! You were always a sharp one,” said Varenukha, grinning spitefully right into the financial director’s face, then unexpectedly sprang from the armchair to the door and quickly pushed down the button of the latch lock. The financial director looked round in despair, backing toward the window that gave onto the garden, and in that window, flooded with moonlight, he saw the face of a naked girl pressed to the glass, and her naked arm, thrust through the small upper pane, trying to open the lower catch. The upper one was already open.

It seemed to Rimsky that the light in the desk lamp was going out and that the desk was tilting. An icy wave broke over Rimsky, but, luckily for him, he mastered himself and did not fall. What remained of his strength was enough for him to whisper, but not to shout:
“Help...”

Varenukha, guarding the door, was hopping up and down beside it, hanging in the air for long moments and swaying there. With crooked fingers he waved toward Rimsky, hissed and smacked his lips, and winked at the girl in the window.

She began to hurry, thrust her red head through the small pane, stretched out her arm as far as she could, began scratching at the lower bolt with her nails and shaking the frame. Her arm started to lengthen, like rubber, and became covered with a corpse-like green. At last the dead woman’s green fingers grasped the head of the bolt, turned it, and the frame began to open. Rimsky gave a weak cry, leaned against the wall, and held out his briefcase in front of him like a shield. He understood that his end had come.

The frame swung wide open, but instead of the freshness of the night and the scent of the lindens, the smell of a cellar burst into the room. The dead woman stepped onto the windowsill. Rimsky clearly saw the spots of decay on her breast.

And at that moment the joyful, unexpected crowing of a rooster came flying from the garden, from that low building behind the shooting gallery where the birds that took part in the shows were kept. The loud-throated trained rooster was trumpeting the news that dawn was rolling toward Moscow from the east.
Wild fury distorted the girl’s face; she let out a hoarse curse, and Varenukha by the door gave a shriek and crashed down out of the air onto the floor.

The rooster crowed again, the girl clacked her teeth, and her red hair stood on end. At the third crow of the rooster she turned and flew out. And after her, springing up and stretching out horizontally in the air, looking like a flying cupid, Varenukha floated slowly out of the window over the desk.

White as snow, without a single dark hair, the old man who only a short while ago had been Rimsky ran to the door, undid the button, opened the door and rushed off along the dark corridor. At the turn to the staircase, moaning with fear, he groped for the switch, and the staircase lit up. On the stairs the shaking, trembling old man fell, because it seemed to him that Varenukha had softly come crashing down on him from above.

Running downstairs, Rimsky saw the watchman, who had fallen asleep on a chair by the box office in the lobby. Rimsky crept past him on tiptoe and slipped out through the main door. In the street he felt somewhat better. He came to his senses so far that, clutching his head, he managed to realize that his hat had been left in the office.

It goes without saying that he did not go back for it but, gasping for breath, ran across the wide street to the opposite corner by the cinema, near which a dim reddish light was hovering. A minute later he was already beside it. Nobody had managed to grab the car first.
“To the Leningrad express, I’ll tip you,” the old man said, breathing heavily and holding his heart.
“I’m going to the garage,” the driver answered with hatred and turned away.
Then Rimsky unbuckled his briefcase, pulled out fifty roubles and held them out to the driver through the open front window.

A few moments later the rattling car was flying like a whirlwind along the Garden Ring. The passenger was tossed about on the seat, and in the shard of mirror hung in front of the driver Rimsky saw now the driver’s joyful eyes, now his own mad ones.
Leaping out of the car in front of the station building, Rimsky shouted to the first man he came across in a white apron, with a badge:
“First class, one, I’ll give you thirty,” crumpling them, he was pulling ten-rouble notes out of his briefcase, “if there’s no first, then second, if there’s none of that, take a hard seat.”
The man with the badge, glancing round at the illuminated clock, was tearing the ten-rouble notes out of Rimsky’s hands.
Five minutes later the express vanished from under the glass dome of the station and disappeared completely into the darkness. And Rimsky disappeared along with it.
